In [[mathematics]], '''relatively hyperbolic groups''' form an important class of [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] of interest for [[geometric group theory]]. The main purpose in their study is to extend the theory of [[Hyperbolic group|Gromov-hyperbolic groups]] to groups <math display="inline">G</math> that may be regarded as [[Hyperbolic metric space|hyperbolic]] assemblies of subgroups <math display="inline">H_i</math>, called peripheral subgroups, in a way that enables "hyperbolic reduction" of problems for <math display="inline">G</math> to problems for the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s.

Illustrative examples of relatively hyperbolic groups are provided by the [[fundamental group]]s of [[complete manifold|complete]] [[compact (topology)|noncompact]] [[hyperbolic manifold]]s of finite volume. Further generalizations such as [[Acylindrically hyperbolic group|acylindrical hyperbolicity]] are also explored by current research.

== Intuition and History ==

Just like Gromov-hyperbolic groups or spaces can be thought of as thickened [[free group]]s or [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]], the idea of a group <math display="inline">G</math> being ''hyperbolic relative'' to a collection of subgroups <math display="inline">H_i</math> (called ''peripheral subgroups'') is that <math display="inline">G</math> looks like a "thickened tree-like patchwork" of the [[Conjugation (group action)|conjugates]] of the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s, so that it is "hyperbolic-away" from them.

From there, different approaches exist and find relevance in different contexts.

The original insight by [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]], motivated by examples from [[Riemannian geometry]] and later elaborated by [[Brian Bowditch|Bowditch]], is to say that <math display="inline">G</math> acts properly, but not cocompactly, on a Gromov-hyperbolic space in such a way that the conjugates of the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s fix points at infinity and that the action becomes cocompact after truncating [[horoball]]s around them. For this reason, the conjugates of the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s are called the ''parabolic subgroups''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gromov |first=Mikhail |date=1987 |title=Hyperbolic groups |journal=Essays in Group Theory. (Seminar Held at the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute, Berkeley, California, June 1985) |volume=8 |pages=75–263 |isbn=0-387-96618-8 |issn=0940-4740}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Bowditch |first=B. H. |date=2012 |title=Relatively hyperbolic groups |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0218196712500166 |journal=International Journal of Algebra and Computation |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=1250016 |doi=10.1142/S0218196712500166 |issn=0218-1967|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Yaman later gave a fully dynamical characterization, no longer involving a hyperbolic space but only its boundary (called the ''Bowditch boundary'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yaman |first=Asli |date=2004 |title=A topological characterisation of relatively hyperbolic groups |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/crll.2004.007/html |journal=Journal für die Reine und Angewandte Mathematik |language=en |volume=2004 |issue=566 |pages=41–89 |doi=10.1515/crll.2004.007 |issn=1435-5345|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The second kind of definition, first due to [[Benson Farb|Farb]], roughly says that after contracting the [[Left coset|left-cosets]] of the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s to bounded sets, the [[Cayley graph]] of <math display="inline">G</math> becomes a (non-proper) Gromov-hyperbolic space.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Farb |first=B. |date=1998-11-01 |title=Relatively Hyperbolic Groups |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s000390050075 |journal=Geometric & Functional Analysis |language=en |volume=8 |issue=5 |pages=810–840 |doi=10.1007/s000390050075 |issn=1420-8970|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The resulting notion, known today as ''weak hyperbolicity'', turns out to require extra assumptions on the behavior of quasi-geodesics in order to match the Gromov-Bowditch one.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Szczepański |first=Andrzej |date=1998 |title=Relatively hyperbolic groups. |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/michigan-mathematical-journal/volume-45/issue-3/Relatively-hyperbolic-groups/10.1307/mmj/1030132303.full |journal=Michigan Mathematical Journal |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=611–618 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1030132303 |issn=0026-2285|arxiv=math/0501321 }}</ref> Bowditch elaborated Farb's definition by only requiring <math display="inline">G</math> to act on a hyperbolic graph with certain additional properties, including that the conjugates of the <math display="inline">H_i</math>s are the infinite vertex stabilizers.<ref name=":0" />

[[Denis Osin|Osin]] later characterized relative hyperbolicity in terms of relative linear isoperimetric inequalities.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Osin |first=Denis V. |date=2006 |title=Relatively hyperbolic groups: intrinsic geometry, algebraic properties, and algorithmic problems |url=http://www.ams.org/books/memo/0843/ |access-date=2025-01-19 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en}}</ref> [[Cornelia Druțu|Druțu]] and [[Mark Sapir|Sapir]] gave a characterization in terms of [[asymptotic cone]]s being [[Tree-graded space|tree-graded metric spaces]], a relative version of [[real tree]]s. This allows for a notion of relative hyperbolicity that makes sense for more general metric spaces than Cayley graphs, and which is invariant by [[quasi-isometry]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Druţu |first1=Cornelia |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark |date=2005-09-01 |title=Tree-graded spaces and asymptotic cones of groups |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0040938305000297 |journal=Topology |volume=44 |issue=5 |pages=959–1058 |doi=10.1016/j.top.2005.03.003 |issn=0040-9383|arxiv=math/0405030 }}</ref>

== Formal definition ==

Given a [[finitely generated group]] ''G'' with Cayley graph ''&Gamma;''(''G'') equipped with the path metric and a subgroup ''H'' of ''G'', one can construct the '''coned off Cayley graph''' <math>\hat{\Gamma}(G,H) </math> as follows:  For each left coset ''gH'', add a vertex  ''v''(''gH'') to the Cayley graph ''&Gamma;''(''G'') and for each element ''x'' of ''gH'', add an edge ''e''(''x'') of length 1/2 from ''x'' to the vertex ''v''(''gH''). This results in a metric space that may not be [[proper metric space|proper]] (i.e. closed balls need not be compact).

The definition of a relatively hyperbolic group, as formulated by [[Brian Bowditch|Bowditch]] goes as follows. A group ''G'' is said to be '''hyperbolic relative to a subgroup ''H'' ''' if the coned off Cayley graph <math> \hat{\Gamma}(G,H) </math> has the properties:
* It is [[δ-hyperbolic space|δ-hyperbolic]] and 
* it is ''fine'': for each integer L, every edge belongs to only finitely many simple cycles of length L.  
If only the first condition holds then the group ''G'' is said to be weakly relatively hyperbolic with respect to ''H''.

The definition of the coned off Cayley graph can be generalized to the case of a collection of subgroups and yields the corresponding notion of relative hyperbolicity. A group ''G'' which contains no collection of subgroups with respect to which it is relatively hyperbolic is said to be a non relatively hyperbolic group.

== Properties ==

* If a group ''G'' is relatively hyperbolic with respect to a hyperbolic group ''H'', then ''G'' itself is hyperbolic.
* If a group ''G'' is relatively hyperbolic with respect to a group ''H'' then it acts as a geometrically finite [[convergence group]] on a compact space, its Bowditch boundary
* If a group ''G'' is relatively hyperbolic with respect to a group ''H'' that has solvable [[word problem (mathematics)|word problem]], then ''G'' has solvable word problem (Farb), and if ''H'' has solvable [[conjugacy problem]], then ''G'' has solvable conjugacy problem (Bumagin)
* If a group ''G'' is torsion-free relatively hyperbolic with respect to a group ''H'', and ''H'' has a finite [[classifying space]], then so does ''G'' (Dahmani)
* If a group ''G'' is relatively hyperbolic with respect to a group ''H'' that satisfies the [[Farrell-Jones conjecture]], then ''G'' satisfies the Farrell-jones conjecture (Bartels).
* More generally, in many cases (but not all, and not easily or systematically), a property satisfied by all hyperbolic groups and by''H'' can be suspected to be satisfied by ''G''
* The [[group isomorphism problem|isomorphism problem]] for virtually torsion-free relatively hyperbolic groups when the peripheral subgroups are finitely generated nilpotent (Dahmani, Touikan)

== Examples ==

* Any [[hyperbolic group]], such as a [[free group]] of finite rank or the fundamental group of a hyperbolic surface, is hyperbolic relative to the trivial subgroup.
* The fundamental group of a [[complete manifold|complete]] [[hyperbolic manifold]] of finite volume is hyperbolic relative to its [[cusp subgroup]].  A similar result holds for any complete finite volume [[Riemannian manifold]] with pinched negative [[sectional curvature]].
* The [[free abelian group]] '''Z'''<sup>2</sup> of rank 2 is weakly hyperbolic, but not hyperbolic, relative to the cyclic subgroup '''Z''': even though the graph <math> \hat{\Gamma}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{Z})</math> is hyperbolic, it is not fine.
* The free product of a group ''H'' with any hyperbolic group, is relatively hyperbolic, relative to ''H''
* Non-abelian [[limit group]]s appearing as limits of free groups are relatively hyperbolic, relative to some free abelian subgroups.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alibegović |first=Emina |last2=Bestvina |first2=Mladen |date=2006 |title=LIMIT GROUPS ARE CAT(0) |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-london-mathematical-society/article/abs/limit-groups-are-cat0/94E11DDA21013A00E2A95883C729FA2E |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=259–272 |doi=10.1112/S0024610706023155 |issn=1469-7750|arxiv=math/0410198 }}</ref>
* Given a semi-direct product of a free group by an infinite cyclic group, it is relatively hyperbolic, relative to some canonical subgroups, if the action of the infinite cyclic group is expanding.
* Combination theorems and small cancellation techniques allow to construct new examples from previous ones.
* The [[mapping class group]] of an orientable finite type [[Surface (topology)|surface]] is either hyperbolic (when 3''g''+''n''<5, where ''g'' is the [[genus (topology)|genus]] and ''n'' is the number of punctures) or is not relatively hyperbolic with respect to any subgroup.
* The [[automorphism group]] and the [[outer automorphism]] group of a free group of finite rank at least 3 are not relatively hyperbolic.
